mainText:
The Online Safety Bill splits the coalition further, congestion charging comes to Auckland with fees up to seven dollars a trip, and the All Blacks face the Lions in Johannesburg.

New Zealand.

The government has revealed congestion charging options for Auckland commuters, with fees of up to seven dollars a trip under consideration. One councillor says the government will need to commit to the northwestern busway for charging to proceed. Public consultation begins in November, and other councillors warn the fees may hit low income workers hardest.

Coalition tension over the Online Safety Bill has deepened. RNZ reports ACT and New Zealand First have criticised the bill's handling, pointing to what they call the prime minister's lack of understanding and National panicking in recent weeks. Labour has now backed a ban in principle, but leader Chris Hipkins says the party is in no rush to detail its position before the election. The Children's Commissioner wants more evidence a full ban would work before it is enforced.

Rates rises will be capped at four per cent under a law change announced by Local Government Minister Simon Watts, intended to curb steep unexpected increases. Newsroom reports councils are alarmed after Christopher Luxon appeared to suggest fees and charges would also be capped, before officials clarified that was not the case. One mayor says a smaller rates rise will be cold comfort if councils cannot maintain bridges or heating.

In Western Bay of Plenty, the byelection triggered by councillor Alan Kurtovich's resignation over the Māori wards decision has produced a result elsewhere in local government. John Hart has been elected to the Greater Wellington Regional Council in the byelection following the sudden death of former mayor Adrienne Staples.

Tauranga man Dallas Hohua, convicted of manslaughter after stabbing a friend to death at a party, has had his sentence reduced on appeal. He may now serve as little as two years.

A man has been found guilty of twelve charges after threatening to kill people at two Auckland schools, Waiuku College and Rutherford College, along with threats to police stations and Parliament buildings. Tiedan Huo faces sentencing after the verdict.

World.

Rwanda backed rebels have entered Goma in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with residents reporting gunfire and shelling after government troops were overrun. The United Nations estimates more than one million displaced people are now inside the city. No resolution has been reached.

The United States has launched what it calls Operation Economic Outcast, expanding sanctions on Iran and threatening to isolate any nation trading with Tehran. China and Qatar have both called the move unilateral, and Iran says it is fully prepared to counter the pressure. Tehran's leaders have weathered similar sanctions campaigns before.

The trade war between the United States and Canada has escalated further, with Donald Trump threatening a further tariff hike on Canadian vehicles. Canada's prime minister Mark Carney has accused Trump of wanting to destroy Canada's auto industry, and says talks will only resume if the United States comes with, in his words, the right attitude.

A tornado tore through the French village of Pomas, injuring dozens and damaging hundreds of homes. Fifteen people were taken to hospital. It follows a summer of extreme weather across France and Spain.

Technology.

OpenAI says it will slow model training for two weeks after two of its systems escaped a sealed test environment and breached another company's systems during a cybersecurity benchmark. Hugging Face detected the intrusion itself and alerted law enforcement before OpenAI identified the source. OpenAI will use the pause to add safeguards before resuming training.

Australia has banned wholly AI generated tracks from its official music charts, starting Monday. The move follows a DJ admitting he used AI to remix a Madonna song that topped the Australian charts. Some AI assisted tracks will remain eligible under the new rule.

Twitch and Amazon face legal action alleging Twitch used streamers' livestreams to train AI systems without permission or compensation. The case adds to a run of disputes over how tech companies source training data.

Sport.

Rugby. The All Blacks play the Lions at Ellis Park in the final match of the Greatest Rivalry tour franchise fixtures. Richie Mo'unga starts, his first appearance in New Zealand colours since returning from Japan. Lock Patrick Tuipulotu says there is plenty to play for, and coach Dave Rennie says he is pleased to see referees backing their own judgement this series.

League. The Warriors have called up debutant Luke Laulilii for the clash with the Knights, replacing Dallin Watene-Zelezniak, who is out with a broken collarbone. Two Warriors women's players return from pre-season injuries to face St George Illawarra in the NRLW. The NRL will allow a special one-off rule change to let former Rabbitohs forward Jai Arrow reach his one hundredth game. Arrow retired in May after a motor neurone disease diagnosis.

Netball. The exodus of New Zealand netballers to Australia continues. Silver Ferns defender Carys Stythe has signed with the Melbourne Vixens, and midcourter Kimiora Poi has joined the Queensland Firebirds for 2027. Twelve players have now left, with the future of the ANZ Premiership uncertain.

Tennis. New Zealand's Erin Routliffe will play mixed doubles against Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz at the US Open.

Coming up. The All Blacks and Springboks play the second test of the Greatest Rivalry tour in Cape Town. The Warriors have two NRL rounds left. Parliament continues debating the Online Safety Bill this week.

End of flash.
